She started her GLP-1 medication at 47. Within six weeks, the woman who danced in our kitchen every Sunday morning stopped coming out of the bathroom.

I'm not exaggerating.

Rachel had fought her weight since our youngest was born. Twelve years of calorie counting. Weight Watchers. Keto. Slimming World. A gym membership she used five days a week for eight months straight.

Nothing worked. Not long enough.

When her GP started her on a GLP-1 medication, it felt like a miracle. The food noise went quiet. The scales moved. She was happy for the first time in years.

Then the constipation started.

At first it was two or three days. She'd mention it casually. "Probably just adjusting."

Then it was five days. She bought Movicol.

Then a week. She added fibre gummies, stool softeners, prune juice.

Then it was ten days.

I found her on the bathroom floor at 11pm on a Tuesday, knees pulled to her chest, tears running down her face.

"I can't do this," she whispered. "It feels like cement inside me. Nothing will move."

That was the moment I stopped trusting what we had been told.

The GP Who Didn't Listen

I went with her to her next appointment.

Dr Sheehan had been her GP for nine years. Good doctor. Thorough. But when Rachel described what was happening, his response made my blood pressure spike.

"Constipation is a common side effect of GLP-1 medications," he said, typing on his laptop. "Are you drinking enough water?"

"She drinks around 2.3 litres a day," I said.

"Fibre?"

"She's taking fibre gummies and Fybogel. They're making her MORE bloated."

He nodded. "Some patients find that fibre can bulk up in a slowed digestive system. Try cutting it back. Add some movement. Walking after meals."

Rachel stared at him. "I walk three miles every morning."

"Give it time," he said. "Most patients adjust."

"It's been two months," I said.

He looked at me with that practised patience doctors use when a partner gets involved.

"The medication is working. She's lost a stone. We need to stay the course." He scribbled on his notepad. "If it gets severe, we can try a prescription laxative. But I'd rather not add another medication."

We left with nothing.

Rachel was quiet the whole drive home.

"He didn't even examine me," she said, staring out the window.

I gripped the steering wheel and didn't answer.

Because she was right.

What I Found at 2am

That night I couldn't sleep.

I sat in the living room with my laptop and started searching. Not the forums. Not the Facebook groups where everyone tells you to drink more water and eat more fibre. I wanted to understand what was actually happening inside her body.

I searched: "why does GLP-1 cause constipation" and "why fibre makes GLP-1 constipation worse."

Most results were the usual advice. Drink more water. Add fibre. Exercise. Everything she was already doing.

Then I found a video from a gastroenterologist who explained something nobody had mentioned.

It wasn't about fibre. It wasn't about water intake.

It was about fuel.

He said your colon doesn't just move on its own. It needs fuel. Specific molecules called short-chain fatty acids, or SCFAs.

He compared it to a car engine.

Your colon runs on SCFAs the way a car runs on petrol. Normally, the bacteria in your gut produce this fuel all day long by fermenting fibre in your colon. That fuel tells your colon to contract and push things through. It feeds the cells that line your colon wall. Without it, your colon sits idle. Like a car with an empty petrol tank.

I paused the video. Stared at the screen.

Then he explained the part that made me want to throw my laptop:

GLP-1 medications slow everything down. That's the point. Slower digestion means you feel full longer, eat less, lose weight.

But the slowdown doesn't just affect your stomach.

It reaches your colon.

When transit slows, the bacteria in your gut get less material to ferment. Less fermentation means less SCFA production. Less fuel for your colon.

And then it spirals.

Slower colon means even less fermentation. Even less fermentation means even less fuel. Even less fuel means an even slower colon. Every day the cycle tightens.

That's why Rachel's constipation was getting WORSE over time. Not better. The cycle couldn't break itself because the medication kept the initial slowdown in place.

I sat there in the dark and felt my chest tighten.

Because suddenly every failed remedy made sense:

Fibre doesn't fix this. Fibre is raw material for the bacteria to ferment. But in a gut that's barely moving, fibre just SITS there. It piles up. It bloats. The factory is shut down. Dumping more raw materials at the door doesn't restart the factory.

Probiotics don't fix this. Probiotics add more bacteria. But those bacteria need to ferment fibre to produce SCFAs. In a slowed gut, they can't do their job. You're hiring workers for a factory with no power.

Laxatives don't fix this. Laxatives force ONE bowel movement by overriding the system. They don't restore fuel production. They push the car downhill once. The tank is still empty tomorrow.

Every single thing Rachel had tried was targeting the wrong problem.

I looked at the bedroom door. She was in there, probably awake, probably bloated, probably wondering if she'd have to quit the medication that finally silenced the food noise.

And I thought: somebody has to be delivering this fuel directly instead of hoping the gut will produce it.

Because that's what she needed. Not more bacteria. Not more fibre. Not more chemical laxatives.

She needed the fuel itself.

The Research That Changed Everything

I kept reading.

I found a clinical study showing that the primary organic acid in fermented kombucha culture is acetic acid. Acetic acid IS acetate. One of the three main SCFAs your colon uses as fuel.

Kombucha doesn't wait for bacteria to ferment fibre into SCFAs. It delivers the fuel molecule directly.

Like pouring petrol into an empty tank instead of waiting for the petrol station to reopen.

Then I found another study. Controlled trial. People consuming kombucha showed improved stool consistency and reduced incomplete bowel evacuation.

A third study showed that specific probiotic strains, L. plantarum and B. coagulans, could survive stomach acid and actually improve motility in constipated adults. B. coagulans reduced indigestion by 65% compared to placebo in a randomised trial.

And then the piece that connected it all:

Dandelion root contains 40% inulin by dry weight. Inulin is a prebiotic that specifically feeds butyrate-producing bacteria. Butyrate provides 70 to 80% of the energy your colon cells need to function.

Slippery elm produces SCFAs during its own breakdown AND coats the gut lining with a protective mucilage.

I sat back and stared at the screen.

The immediate problem: her colon was starving for fuel. Kombucha delivers that fuel directly.

The long-term problem: her gut bacteria couldn't produce their own fuel. Prebiotics and targeted probiotics rebuild that production line.

Both problems. One approach. Fuel delivery now. Factory rebuild over time.

I woke Rachel up.

"I found something," I said.

She looked at me with that tired, hollowed-out expression I'd been seeing for weeks.

"Nate," she said. "Please. I can't handle another thing that doesn't work."

"This is different. Everything you've tried was targeting the wrong problem. Your colon is starving for a specific fuel. And there's one thing that delivers it directly."

She didn't say anything for a long time.

Then: "What do we have to lose?"

What Happened When She Tried It

The next morning I started researching.

I needed something that combined kombucha culture with prebiotics and the right probiotic strains. Not just a basic probiotic capsule. Not just kombucha in a bottle.

Most gut supplements for people on GLP-1 medications are rubbish.

Standard probiotics use strains that die in the stomach, especially with the delayed emptying from a GLP-1. The bacteria sit in acid for hours and never reach the colon alive.

Fibre supplements dump more bulk into an already stalled system.

Cheap kombucha drinks are mostly sugar water with trace amounts of culture.

I found one company that combined the right things:

Kombucha powder delivering direct SCFAs. L. plantarum and B. coagulans, both proven to survive stomach acid and improve motility. Dandelion root and slippery elm for prebiotic support and gut lining protection.

It was called Glissé. Organic-certified. Third-party tested. They published their Certificate of Analysis right on the site.

I almost scrolled past it. The website didn't look like the big supplement brands.

But the formulation matched exactly what the research said her colon needed.

I ordered a bottle.

I didn't tell Rachel. I didn't want to get her hopes up again.

When it arrived three days later, I waited until evening.

She was sitting on the sofa, hot water bottle on her stomach, looking miserable. She'd skipped dinner because eating made the bloating worse.

"Try these," I said, handing her the bottle.

She looked at me. Then at the bottle.

"What is it?"

"Kombucha gummies. With prebiotics and probiotics designed for people on GLP-1 medications."

That tired, sceptical look. The one that said: We've been through this before.

"Two gummies," I said. "That's it. If nothing happens in two weeks, we stop."

She took two gummies. Chewed them. Made a face that said "not bad." Went back to her hot water bottle.

I didn't expect much that night.

Week One: "Something Feels Different"

The first three days, nothing.

Day four, Rachel said something at breakfast that made me look up from my coffee.

"I feel less... stuck."

"What do you mean?"

"I don't know. Like things are moving. A little."

Day five, she had a bowel movement. Not dramatic. Not the explosive Movicol-driven kind that left her cramping for hours. Just... normal. Quiet.

She came out of the bathroom and looked at me.

"That's the first time in three weeks it didn't hurt," she said.

I didn't say anything. Too early. Could be coincidence.

Day six. Another one. No straining. No pain.

Day seven. Same.

I was paying attention now.

Week Two: "I Forgot About My Stomach"

By the end of the second week, the change was undeniable.

Rachel was eating dinner with me again. Full portions. No hot water bottle afterwards.

The bloating that had made her look six months pregnant since starting the medication was visibly reduced. She put on a pair of jeans she hadn't worn in two months.

"They fit," she said, sounding confused. "They actually fit."

But the thing that got me was what she said Thursday evening.

We were watching TV. She turned to me.

"I forgot about my stomach today."

"What?"

"I went through the whole day and didn't think about my stomach once. I didn't plan my meals around whether I'd bloat. I didn't avoid eating because I was scared of the pain. I just... ate. And was fine."

She paused.

"I can't remember the last time that happened."

Week Four: "I Feel Like Myself Again"

A month in, Rachel woke me up early on a Saturday.

"Let's go to the farmers' market," she said. "I want to walk around. I want to eat something from one of the stands and not worry about it."

We hadn't done that in four months.

We spent the whole morning together. She tried a peach from a vendor and laughed when the juice ran down her chin. She bought herbs for a recipe she'd been too sick to make.

Walking home, she looped her arm through mine.

"I feel like myself again," she said.

Then, quieter: "I didn't realise how bad it had gotten until it stopped."

I didn't say anything. I just held her arm tighter.

Week Six: Dr Sheehan's Appointment

Rachel had a routine follow-up with Dr Sheehan.

I went with her.

When the nurse asked about her medications, Rachel mentioned the Glissé gummies.

Dr Sheehan pulled up her chart. "How are the digestive symptoms?"

"Gone," Rachel said. "Daily bowel movements. No bloating. No pain."

He looked up from his screen. "Gone?"

"I've been taking a fermented kombucha supplement with prebiotics. My husband found research about how GLP-1 medications can starve the colon of the fuel it needs to move."

Dr Sheehan looked at his notes. Then back at Rachel.

"Well," he said. "Your weight loss is continuing. You're tolerating the medication. And the constipation has resolved."

Pause.

"I'm not familiar with that particular connection. But your results speak for themselves. Continue what you're doing."

That was the best we were going to get. And honestly? It was enough.

Why Most Gut Supplements for GLP-1 Users Don't Work

After Rachel's results, I told three women at her gym who were dealing with the same thing.

Two of them tried generic probiotics from Amazon.

Nothing changed.

I wasn't surprised. Because I'd already learned this the hard way:

Most probiotics do NOT work for people on GLP-1 medications. The delayed stomach emptying means bacteria sit in acid for hours. Most strains die before reaching the colon. You're swallowing dead bacteria.

And even the ones that survive? They need to ferment fibre to produce SCFAs. In a slowed gut, that fermentation barely happens. The workers show up but the factory has no power.

Glissé was the only supplement I found that delivers SCFAs directly through kombucha culture AND includes spore-forming probiotics that actually survive GLP-1 stomach conditions AND has the prebiotics to rebuild the gut's own fuel production over time.

That's why it works. And that's why the cheap alternatives don't.

If Your Wife, Partner, or Someone You Love Is on a GLP-1 Medication, Please Read This

Ask yourself:

If you said yes to even one of those, it's not "just adjusting."

I didn't want a chemical evacuation on a timer. I wanted my own body working again, the way it had my whole life.

Quitting the shot was never on the table. Go off it and the weight comes back. I'd watched too many patients do exactly that. Square one.

So I stayed backed up. Seven, eight, nine days of nothing. Bloated like I'd swallowed rocks, and scared of where it was heading.

I've been a nurse too long to chase every fix that gets passed around online. I'd about made my peace that this was just my life now.

Then about two months ago, one of my regular patients came in for her appointment. Sweet lady on Mounjaro for the past few months. She'd been struggling with constipation the entire time - two months of living off laxatives, miserable.

But this time she seemed different. More relaxed somehow.

I asked her how she was managing, and she said something I didn't expect. She told me she was actually going regularly now. She'd found this tea - oolong tea - with natural antioxidants and gentle caffeine. Been drinking it every morning. And for the first time in months, she was having normal bowel movements. No cramping. No laxatives. No fear.

I'll be honest, I was very skeptical. I've heard every miracle cure story you can imagine. But she seemed so genuinely relieved. Like she'd finally found something that actually worked.

That same night, I was on day 8 without a bowel movement. My stomach was so distended I couldn't sleep comfortably. I laid there feeling bloated and genuinely scared. And I kept thinking about what she'd said. So I looked it up.

Turns out, the antioxidants in oolong tea - along with natural caffeine and L-theanine - support digestive motility and gut microbiome health naturally. When it arrived, I made a cup that first morning. I didn't expect much. Just another thing to try.

After about a week, things started moving a little. From once a week to every 4-5 days. Better. But not life-changing.

So I ordered a different brand. This one was cheaper, came in tea bags instead of loose leaf. After two weeks, things stayed about the same. Maybe every 3-4 days. Still too uncomfortable.

I was getting frustrated. Everyone said oolong tea worked. But it wasn't working for me.

One person said they tried three different brands before finding one that actually worked. Another mentioned most oolong tea you can buy online is "tea dust" - the broken leftover scraps from processing that don't have any of the actual healing compounds.

I started researching. Turns out, most oolong teas are:

\- Over-processed (which destroys the polyphenols)

\- Grown at low elevations (weaker potency)

\- Mixed with tea dust and fillers

\- Sprayed with pesticides

\- Machine-harvested (damages the leaves)

The oolong teas that actually worked for digestive support had to be:

\- Whole leaf (not dust or broken pieces)

\- Grown above 4,500 feet (higher altitude = more potent polyphenols)
